slides.title: From World War II to Continuation War
slides.body: World War II created the conditions for Finland to renew its struggle with the Soviet Union. After losing territory in the Winter War, Finland aligned militarily with Germany as Operation Barbarossa began. Finnish leaders sought to recover the lost regions, turning the conflict into the Continuation War.

stats.lbl: World War II created the conditions for Finland to renew its struggle with the Soviet Union. After losing territory in the Winter War, Finland aligned militarily with Germany as Operation Barbarossa began. Finnish leaders sought to recover the lost regions, turning the conflict into the Continuation War.

slides.title: Peace Without Security
slides.body:
The Moscow Peace Treaty ended the Winter War but left Finland wounded and anxious. Karelia had been ceded, hundreds of thousands were displaced, and many Finns feared the Soviet Union would return to finish what it had started.

Drifting Toward Germany: Britain and France were unable to guarantee Finnish security, while the Soviet threat remained close. Finland gradually accepted military cooperation and transit arrangements with Germany, a dangerous alignment born from fear and strategic isolation.

title: Barbarossa and Finland's Entry
sub: A Separate War Begins Beside Germany

slides.title: Germany Invades the Soviet Union
slides.body:
On 22 June 1941, Germany launched Operation Barbarossa. Finland allowed German forces to operate from its territory, and Soviet aircraft bombed Finnish cities days later. Finland declared that it was again at war with the Soviet Union.

Co-Belligerent, Not Axis Member: Finland fought alongside Germany against the Soviet Union but did not sign the Tripartite Pact. Finnish leaders described the war as a limited struggle to regain lost territory and secure the state, though cooperation with Nazi Germany deeply shaped the conflict.

slides.title: The Army Moves East
slides.body:
Finnish forces attacked across the old border and rapidly retook much of the territory lost in 1940. For many soldiers and evacuees, the campaign felt like a recovery of stolen homes rather than a war of conquest.

Beyond the Old Border: Finland also advanced into East Karelia beyond the 1939 border, raising difficult questions about war aims. Some saw a chance to build a Greater Finland; others worried that moving too far tied Finland more tightly to Germany's war.

slides.title: A City Under Siege
slides.body:
Germany encircled Leningrad from the south while Finnish forces held positions to the north. Finland did not launch a major assault into the city, but its presence helped close the ring around one of the war's most catastrophic sieges.

Limited War Aims Tested: Finnish leaders tried to balance military cooperation with Germany against their own limited goals. Refusing a direct assault on Leningrad preserved some independence of action, but Finland remained tied to a brutal Axis campaign in the east.

title: Occupation of East Karelia
sub: Military Rule Beyond Finland's Old Border

markers.label: Petrozavodsk

markers.label: East Karelia

slides.title: A Finnish Military Administration
slides.body:
In East Karelia, Finland established military rule over territory that had not belonged to independent Finland. Officials treated Finnic populations differently from Russians, reflecting ethnic nationalist ideas that shaped occupation policy.

Camps and Hardship: Thousands of civilians were held in camps during the occupation, and many suffered from hunger, disease, and forced displacement. The occupation remains one of the darkest parts of Finland's wartime history.

title: Static War and Home Front
sub: A Long Pause Before the Storm

slides.title: War of Positions
slides.body:
After the 1941 advances, the front became largely static. Soldiers built trenches, bunkers, and supply lines through forest and swamp. The war did not stop, but it settled into patrols, artillery, raids, and waiting.

A Country Under Strain: Finland's home front lived with rationing, air raids, displaced families, and dependence on German food and arms. The longer the war lasted, the harder it became to believe Germany would win or that Finland could escape the consequences easily.

slides.title: A Massive Soviet Attack
slides.body:
In June 1944, the Red Army launched a major offensive against Finland while Germany was collapsing elsewhere. Soviet artillery, armor, and air power smashed through forward positions on the Karelian Isthmus, forcing a rapid Finnish retreat.

Finland Seeks Weapons and Time: Finland urgently requested German anti-tank weapons, aircraft support, and ammunition. The crisis forced Finnish leaders to balance the need for German help with the growing need to exit the war before Soviet terms became worse.

markers.label: Tali-Ihantala
markers.description: Tali-Ihantala marks Finland's largest battle and a key defensive success in 1944.

markers.label: Vyborg / Viipuri
markers.description: Vyborg / Viipuri marks the nearby city whose loss preceded the defensive stand.

slides.title: The Largest Nordic Battle
slides.body:
At Tali-Ihantala, Finnish forces concentrated artillery, anti-tank weapons, and air support to stop repeated Soviet assaults. The battle became the largest fought in the Nordic countries and the decisive defensive success of Finland's 1944 crisis.

A Defensive Victory: The Soviet advance was halted before it could break into Finland's interior. Tali-Ihantala did not restore lost territory, but it strengthened Finland's hand in peace negotiations by proving that occupation would be costly.

slides.title: Hard Terms, Independence Preserved
slides.body:
Finland signed the Moscow Armistice in September 1944. It accepted the 1940 territorial losses, ceded Petsamo, paid reparations, legalized previously banned political groups, and agreed to expel German troops from its territory.

Turning Against Germany: One armistice condition required Finland to remove German forces. This transformed Finland's former partner into its next enemy and led directly to the Lapland War in the north.

slides.title: A Narrow Escape
slides.body:
Finland ended the war defeated but not occupied. It lost territory, paid reparations, and accepted Soviet influence, yet preserved parliamentary institutions and avoided the fate of many Eastern European states brought under direct Soviet domination.

A Complicated War Story: The Continuation War is remembered as a struggle for national survival, but also as a conflict fought beside Nazi Germany and involving occupation beyond Finland's old borders. Its legacy is one of endurance, compromise, and unresolved moral tension.
slides.cap: Karelian evacuees remained one of the war's lasting human consequences

stats.lbl: Finland learns to live beside the USSR

slides.title: War Summary: Continuation War
slides.cap: Karelian evacuees remained one of the war's lasting human consequences
slides.body: Finland accepted an armistice, restored the post-Winter War border with further concessions, and expelled German forces. It survived as an independent democracy under strong Soviet pressure.
